paragraphs.heading: The law in one line
paragraphs.text: Conservation of momentum says that the total momentum of a closed system never changes. A closed system here means one that trades no matter with its surroundings and has no outside forces acting on it. Momentum itself is mass times velocity, p = mv, and it has both a size and a direction.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is true
paragraphs.text: The law follows from Newton's laws of motion. Imagine two particles acting on each other. Newton's third law says those two forces have equal size and point opposite ways. By the second law, each force equals the rate at which that particle's momentum changes, so one particle's momentum rises exactly as fast as the other's falls.

paragraphs.heading: Adding it up
paragraphs.text: Because the two changes cancel, the sum p₁ + p₂ stays fixed, which is written d/dt(p₁ + p₂) = 0. Put in terms of masses and velocities, the total of mass times velocity for the two particles is the same before and after they interact. This works however complicated the force between the particles is.

paragraphs.heading: Many particles at once
paragraphs.text: With more than two particles, the same idea applies to every pair. The momentum swapped within each pair adds to zero, so the total change is zero. Across the whole group, the sum of each mass times its velocity stays constant.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing a viewpoint
paragraphs.text: The value of momentum depends on the frame of reference you measure from. In any inertial frame, though, the total is conserved. And since momentum points in a direction, it helps predict how fast and which way objects move once they collide.

paragraphs.heading: A deep symmetry
paragraphs.text: The law expresses a basic symmetry of space and time known as translational symmetry. It survives, in modified forms, in special relativity, electrodynamics, quantum mechanics, quantum field theory and general relativity. Even fluids and electromagnetic fields have a momentum per unit volume that obeys a conservation law. For fluids, this leads to the Navier–Stokes equations.
